absent: Full struct definitions, field order, sizes, alignment and padding for the virtual CPU, virtual machine, local APIC, MMU, page walk, role and format objects.
Locking and lifetime rules beyond the single virtual CPU assertion, including what guards APIC registers, MMU roots, CPUID data, irqchip mode and Hyper-V state.
Numeric application binary interface values such as register offsets, version codes, flag bit positions, shifts, masks and table dimensions.
Bodies and contracts of callees not routed here, including register stores, fault handlers, synchronization callbacks, permission and protection-key updaters, table readers and address translators.
CPUID lookup, guest capability checks, host capability discovery and global control lifecycles for paging mode, depth limits, masks and tracking switches.
Effects of enabling Hyper-V CPUID state beyond the no-op setter and the state-pointer accessor.
Interrupt-controller mode lifecycle, writers, ordering and split versus full semantics beyond the presence tests.
System-management and guest-mode flag lifecycle and the full host-flags layout.
Error handling, return codes, concurrency behavior and performance characteristics of the shown paths.
Guest paging metadata details beyond the rebuild triggers, including protection-key mask derivation and nested-walk selection.

findings.text: The helper named to_hv_vcpu exposes the per virtual CPU Hyper-V state pointer held in the architecture portion of the virtual CPU object, first asserting that the caller holds the virtual CPU lock or that the virtual CPU is unreachable.
A virtual CPU may be touched only while its mutex is held or while it is unreachable, where unreachable means its index is negative or its owning virtual machine has no counted users.
The inline routine named kvm_hv_set_cpuid accepts a virtual CPU and an enable flag and has no observable effect in these fragments.

The routine named kvm_apic_set_version is an externally visible entry that refreshes the local APIC version register for a virtual CPU and does nothing when the local APIC is handled outside the kernel.

The version value combines a base version identifier with a field derived from the configured local APIC vector table entry count, and adds the directed end-of-interrupt marker only when the guest advertises extended APIC mode and the virtual machine advertises broadcast suppression; the result is stored through the register-store helper.

Broadcast-suppression advertisement follows a three-way mode on the virtual machine: an enabled mode always advertises, a disabled mode never advertises, and a quirked mode advertises only when the input-output APIC is handled outside the kernel; any other mode raises a one-time warning and does not advertise.

Whether the input-output APIC lives in the kernel is decided by the full-irqchip test; one build compares the virtual machine irqchip mode against the kernel value after an ordering barrier, while an alternate build always reports the chipset as outside the kernel.
Local APIC in-kernel presence is normally true; under the no-APIC static branch it instead follows whether the per virtual CPU APIC pointer is present.

The routines named kvm_mmu_after_set_cpuid, kvm_mmu_reset_context and kvm_init_mmu are externally visible MMU entries: the first reacts to CPUID changes, the second unloads and rebuilds paging state, and the third rebuilds role-derived paging state from current registers.

After CPUID data changes both the root and guest page-role validity markers are discarded and both nested address-translation walks are marked invalid before the context is rebuilt, because CPUID feeds reserved-bit computation; the sequence then requires that the virtual CPU still permit CPUID and feature register updates.

MMU initialization derives role register values from control registers, folds them into a CPU paging role, always refreshes the guest-virtual walk, and when the virtual CPU is not already using the nested guest MMU it selects either the two-dimensional paging path or the shadow paging path according to a global enable flag.
Nesting is reported exactly when the active MMU pointer of the virtual CPU aliases its guest MMU object.

Role register values are built from masked reads of the paging-related control registers together with the extended feature register; the masked control-register read refreshes its cached value when guest-owned bits intersect the requested mask while the register cache is not already available.

The CPU paging role starts with full access plus system-management and guest-mode flags and a validity marker; with paging disabled it is marked direct and returned, otherwise it records paging-level, protection-key, address-width and protection-flag attributes derived from the role registers together with a fetch-fault capability derived from execute-disable and supervisor-mode-execution-protection state.
Guest mode and system-management mode are each read as masked bits from the host-flags word of the virtual CPU; one system-management build always reports false instead of testing the flag.

Two-dimensional paging initialization computes a candidate root page role and leaves the context untouched when its word is unchanged; on change it stores the new role, selects the two-dimensional fault handler, clears the synchronization callback, and refreshes both the permission bitmap and the reserved-bit masks.

The two-dimensional root role is direct with full supervisor access, forced write-protect and execute-disable semantics, host-derived supervisor-mode-execution protection, system-management and guest-mode flags copied from the CPU role, access-dirty tracking inverted from a global switch, a level from the TDP level query, and user access removed when supervisor-mode-execution protection coexists with a nonzero user mask.

The TDP paging depth for confidential guests comes from a CPUID-derived maximum guest physical address width and otherwise from the CPU maximum physical address width; an architecturally forced root depth wins when nonzero, otherwise the configured maximum depth applies with a reduction from the widest to the narrower long-mode depth when the address width fits.
The maximum guest physical address width is read from the appropriate extended CPUID leaf field when the prerequisite leaves exist, and zero is returned when they are absent.

Reserved-bit masks are maintained per leaf category and per paging depth from the host reserved physical-address bits, combined with execute-disable, large-page and vendor-specific rules that differ between the AMD-style table builder and the extended-page-table builder, with an additional memory-encryption carve-out applied level by level when its mask is active.

The page-size-extension width probe unconditionally reports true in these fragments, and the AMD boot-CPU probe is valid only while two-dimensional paging is enabled, selecting the AMD-style reserved-bit builder versus the extended-page-table builder.

The extended-page-table mask builder reserves high address bits plus per-depth control-bit ranges, gates gigantic and large page-table-entry size bits by the supported huge-page depth, and builds a separate illegal memory-type and write-execute combination bitmap whose execute-only treatment depends on its flag.

Permission bitmaps are indexed by a shifted fault-code value and record, for every access combination, whether read, write, user, fetch or supervisor-mode-access-prevention rules fault; the extended-table path keys fetch faults off supervisor and user execute masks with an optional user distinction, while the other path additionally honors write-protect, execute-disable, supervisor-mode-execution protection and supervisor-mode-access prevention with a nested-paging exception.

Shadow MMU setup derives its root from the CPU base role with a minimum paging-depth floor and forced execute-disable semantics, then dispatches the context among nonpaging and two paging flavors according to paging and address-extension state; an unchanged role word leaves the context untouched, otherwise fault and synchronization callbacks plus permission and reserved-bit tables are refreshed.
Paging is considered active when the walk CPU role reports a positive depth, and address-extension paging is considered active when guest page-table entries are not of the short four-byte form.

Guest page-walk setup caches the CPU role and returns early when it is unchanged; on change it installs fault-injection and table-access callbacks, selects among direct and two paging address translators by paging mode, and when paging is active rebuilds guest reserved-bit, permission and protection-key metadata.

Guest reserved-bit masks are rebuilt from the per virtual CPU reserved guest-address bits, the walk paging depth, execute-disable and page-size-extension state, guest gigantic-page capability, and an AMD-compatibility marker cached on the virtual CPU.

Observed object relationships place a mutex, an index and an owning-machine pointer on the virtual CPU, an architecture area holding Hyper-V state, local APIC state, MMU objects and walks, control-register images and flag words, and on the machine a user count plus architecture fields for irqchip mode and broadcast-suppression mode, with the APIC object carrying its register image and vector-table size.

Observed paging objects pair each MMU with a root-role word, fault and synchronization callbacks and a format block holding reserved-bit masks, a permission table and an illegal-combination bitmap, while each walk pairs a cached CPU role with translation and metadata callbacks and its own format block; roles separate a base paging-attribute group from an extended validity and feature group.
Named application binary interface markers identify the local APIC version register, its base version value, the vector-table-count field placement, and the directed end-of-interrupt flag.

Named paging-depth and protection markers distinguish legacy, extended and long-mode table depths and the associated execute-disable, write-protect, execution-protection, access-prevention, size-extension and address-width attributes used by role derivation and mask builders.

Named fault-code bits for write, user, fetch, present and reserved conditions and named access combinations for read, write, execute and user permissions form the index and value vocabulary of the permission tables.

Unexpected broadcast-suppression modes, shadow roots below the minimum depth, and AMD probes issued while two-dimensional paging is disabled each trigger a one-time warning path and fall back to denying advertisement, keeping prior state, or treating the CPU as non-AMD respectively.
The CPUID-change path ends in a host-bug check that the virtual CPU still allows CPUID and feature-register updates after its paging state has been invalidated and rebuilt.

The APIC version setter, the MMU CPUID-change hook, the MMU context reset helper, the MMU initializer and the guest address-width query are non-static routines available across objects in these fragments.
